key_insight: Base models can often reason much better if the prompt starts with cue tokens they have implicitly associated with “reasoning mode” during training. The paper shows that simple fixed starters like “Okay” or “Alright,” can sharply boost math and coding accuracy, sometimes rivaling RL-trained models.
problem_solved: This work addresses the gap between strong reasoning performance in RL-trained models and weaker performance in base models. It asks whether some of that gap is due not only to training objective changes, but also to learned associations between response prefixes and downstream reasoning behavior.
method: Analyze how specific beginning-of-response token cues affect a base model’s reasoning quality.
Fix different starter phrases and measure changes in benchmark performance on math and coding tasks.
Compare cue-conditioned base model results against RL-trained counterparts to assess how much of the performance gap can be closed.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests that prompting and data-induced cueing can unlock much of a base model’s latent reasoning ability without additional alignment training. It can reduce reliance on costly RL pipelines and improve how models are prompted, evaluated, and deployed.
visual_elements: A before/after bar chart showing benchmark accuracy with and without starter-token cues.
A pipeline diagram linking training data -> cue association -> reasoning behavior.
A token prefix callout panel highlighting example cues like “.\n\nOkay” and “Alright,”.
A side-by-side comparison of base model vs RL-trained model performance on math/coding tasks.
paper_title: Base Models Can Reason By Taking a Cue From Training Data
paper_authors: Sophie L. Wang, Amil Dravid, Rulin Shao, Kevin Farhat, Sewon Min
